To showcase the effectiveness of this framework, we design a specific GFNN to complement a well-established GCNN, the Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN). Through a comparative analysis of GFNN and MPNN, we showcase the distinctive characteristics of each and showcase the versatility of our graphical signal processing framework by matching specific MPNN filters with corresponding GFNN filters. This analysis highlights the distinct filters used by each method, revealing that MPNN relies on operation-specific filters, whereas GFNN uses a small set of base filters to generate a wide range of graph filters. Our empirical evaluations with six benchmark datasets showcase the impressive signal processing capabilities of our GCNN framework, while our analysis demonstrates that there is often a notable correlation between the filter weights used by both the MPNN and GFNN. Moreover, we observe that the signal processing output of the GFNN provides a more comprehensive representation of the input graph compared to the MPNN, as evidenced by higher evaluation metrics in our empirical evaluations.

Universal dependencies represent part-of-speech and dependency relations across languages in a standardized format, facilitating cross-lingual comparisons and training models on data scarce languages using data abundant ones as a reference. Despite the benefits, training models on complete UD datasets from multiple languages under a single framework is impractical due to the requirement for unified annotations. In our research, we utilize a contextualized model to implicitly learn part-of-speech and dependency analyses without needing explicit annotations on all sentences. This self-learning approach is effective when there is at least one fully annotated sentence in a document. Furthermore, when there is no complete sentence with parts of several sentences merged, our model can learn dependencies by utilizing fully annotated paragraphs. This model's results compare favorably to traditional models in multiple data scarce languages. In our experiments, a contextualized self-learning model was able to achieve 42 new UD languages' quality scores of 92 plus/minus 2, whereas the current best performance on 42 new UD languages is at 89 plus/minus 2. Furthermore, our model's performance increased by 8 and 5 F measure on average in BERT and StanfordCoreNLP baseline models respectively in data scarce languages.

The representation of hadronic matrix elements in terms of the momentum fractions of the valence quarks, $x$, offers a natural framework to study hadron structure using light-front quantization. By applying this framework to the $B\to D$ transition and analyzing the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ decay process, researchers have fitted the data on the shape factors $R_X$ and $R_2$ with the light-front quark model without any free parameters. Interestingly, the results show that $R_X$ and $R_2$ depend heavily on the momentum fraction $x$ and vary significantly between different light-front quark models. Additionally, the study found that the $B\to D$ transition is highly $x$-dependent but the average value is around 0.55, confirming the $x$-dependent nature of the transition. The detailed examination of the shape factors highlights the potential of $R_X$ and $R_2$ in determining the distribution of the momentum among the valence quarks in the $B\to D$ transition.

By building upon existing concepts of reversible and irreversible branes, researchers have expanded the notion of symmetry to encompass non-reversible branes. This expanded definition encompasses both reversible and irreversible branes as well as certain novel types of branes. Utilizing the example of coset branes, which are constructed from Lie groups using algebraic structures, the difference between reversible and irreversible branes is elucidated in detail. The study further examines the relationship between cosmic string-like branes and algebraic structures, revealing a distinct aspect of non-reversible branes that cannot be applied to reversible branes. Furthermore, researchers have derived equations governing the dynamical movement of branes through a substrate using a quantum correction approach. This movement is found to be subject to a dual constraint in relation to a homotopy algebra operation.

Cai, Furer, and Immerman proposed a hypothesis about undirected graphs and two variables, stating that they can be recognized with a logarithmic space complexity on deterministic Turing machines. A simpler model, the probabilistic monotone planar graph property tester, is equivalent to log-space complexity for general undirected graphs with two variables. Our research demonstrates that recognizing graphs with the property in either model is possible in acyclic zero-redundancy contexts with a polynomial duration in the size of the input.

In a comprehensive investigation, we explored how the insulating properties of Bi-doped Eu2Ir2O7 change as the amount of Bi doping varies, using a unique combination of theory and experimental High-energy Photoemission Spectroscopy. Our results show that Bi doping causes significant displacement of Eu ions, leading to a gradual increase in metal-like characteristics on the Eu 4f core level. This suggests an insulator-to-metal transition is not the primary effect of Bi doping in this system, instead, it can be attributed to an increased number of metal-like states at the Fermi level on the Eu ions, alongside increased disorder. This explanation is supported by our calculation of the insulating barrier in the Eu-Bi system, which shows that Bi doping increases the overlap between adjacent states within the insulating phase, thus disrupting it. Additionally, our findings on the Bi-Bi vacancy system reveal that local insulating phases coexist with conducting material, separated by very thin zones. This is corroborated by both our experimental observations and theoretical model, which both indicate that Bi-Bi vacancy systems have a unique structural arrangement in the top layer. In summary, our research has shown that Bi doping into Eu2Ir2O7 causes metal-like states to appear on Eu ions and increases disorder, while also creating conducting material within an insulating environment. This is facilitated by an insulating barrier that is disrupted by Bi doping, which also results in unique Bi-Bi vacancy structures with conducting material separated by thin

The concept of a set-valued function's heart, or core, provides a pivotal framework for studying multivariate mapping properties. Specifically, it allows we to examine when a two-dimensional set-valued function exhibits a limited increase in dimension when subjected to a perturbation. Furthermore, it plays a key role in addressing questions surrounding its Lipschitz property. Our research focuses on set-valued functions with compact images of a bounded and low-dimensional nature. An important finding is that, contrary to expectations, such functions may not possess a Lipschitz property, even if they have relatively smooth charts and are defined over a simple graph. This discovery highlights the significance of the core in establishing the criteria for a Lipschitz property. Moreover, it emphasizes the value of considering singularities and geometric constraints when analyzing multivariate mapping properties. Ultimately, our study leads to the development of new algorithms that efficiently utilize the core's existence.

The comparison of complex datasets often relies on likelihoods that cannot be easily compared directly, necessitating the use of likelihood ratios or posterior proportions in Bayesian analysis. This work explores the properties of circular and nonnegative likelihoods, building on a previous investigation of additive models. The new insights enable the identification of a broad class of models that can be consistently compared, encompassing circular and nonnegative likelihood models, as well as certain models with zero-normed penalties. The results are illustrated with examples from Bayesian variable selection, sparse canonical correlation analysis, and covariance-based clustering.

In dynamic compilation environments, the majority of the overhead occurs during program execution, caused by the time-consuming process of creating a native code image. Various techniques have been developed to mitigate this issue, such as generating compaction units, employing portable and component-based structure formats, and optimizing runtime configuration processes. A novel method for reducing runtime setup complexity is presented in this paper, where the overhead of processing initialization data and external library dependencies during program startup is minimized by shifting the configuration process to the compilation stage. An exhaustive evaluation of this method was conducted across a range of programs, libraries, and configuration scenarios. The results reveal that the runtime setup time can be entirely eliminated in most cases, and when necessary, the remaining overhead accounts for no more than 1% of program startup time. Furthermore, the experiment demonstrated that the proposed method is applicable to a broad spectrum of programs, yielding a high success rate of 87.1%. The associated costs of increased compilation time and memory requirements pose no significant obstacle, as the ratios of these expenses to program startup time stand at 3.25% and 0.97%, respectively.

We propose a novel strategy to directly detect sub-GeV dark matter through the observation of electron collisions produced in heavy ion collisions. Since electrons lack a neutrino partner when emitted from the center of the nucleus, they serve as more reliable signals for dark matter interaction. We demonstrate that a specialized electron spectrometer alongside a reliable electron source can distinguish dark matter-induced electrons from background collisions. This detection method is expected to yield substantial gains in sensitivity, surpassing current direct detection equipment capabilities. In our study, we explore the detection potential of the J-PET experiment and future large-scale facilities like the electron-ion collider.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-level system interacting with a cavity mode in the presence of continuous wave emission, describing the system with a Markovian master equation. We investigate the entanglement between the two-level system and the cavity mode, and observe that entanglement transmission is possible only when the two-level system is initially in a superposition state. Furthermore, we find that for specific initial states, the cavity mode exhibits Rabi oscillations in two-level system-emitter separability, and explore the influence of emission rate and Rabi frequency on this phenomenon.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide insights into a person's cardiovascular system, helping doctors detect irregularities such as arrhythmias. However, identifying these intervals from noisy signals in difficult environments can be challenging for doctors and lead to inaccurate readings. To tackle this problem, a solution using the Tiramisu framework for ECG signal denoising has been implemented. The approach relies on a custom-designed network to analyze ECG signals and an adapted loss function that focuses on beat-to-beat consistency, enabling accurate measurements even from poorly quality signals. The proposed method surpasses existing techniques in terms of accuracy, according to tests with a dataset of ECG signals recorded from individuals with irregular heartbeats in difficult environments.

We analyze an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle model, where many similar particles are present in a potential field with realistic simulations of labor (active propulsion forces against viscosity resistance) represented by a force equation. This force equation depends on the particle's location, velocity, and a set of interaction parameters that represent interactions between particles and their surroundings. By adjusting these parameters, we can observe a wide range of particle behaviors, from collective movement patterns to increased activity levels. We perform detailed analyses of the system's dynamics, focusing on labor-dependent phase diagrams and the transition times between different states. Our study reveals that adjusting the parameters results in different regimes of behavior, such as collective movement, increased movement, and labor-dependent movement patterns. Our results provide a foundation for further research on more complex systems involving multiple particles.

This paper presents HUMBI, a comprehensive multiview dataset consisting of various gaze patterns, which can be utilized to create synthetic training datasets for neural network development. By photographing subjects performing a diverse range of movements, the dataset captures unique viewing angles. HUMBI's size enables it to be downloadable in its entirety. In conjunction with HUMBI, we are introducing a competition, known as HUMBI Challenge, to assess the performance of neural networks in generating human body movements. In the near future, more details about the competition will be available on Codevision.

We've developed a model-independent framework for crossing linguistic boundaries in NLU tasks. This approach relies on a pre-trained multilingual language model and a task depiction, which is a compact representation of the task defined by experts. The key innovation here is the use of task depictions as flexible guides for adapting the pre-trained model to new, unseen tasks across different languages. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through robust results on a range of 8 low-resource languages and 14 high-resource ones, outperforming the current best multilingual model by a significant margin in many cases. Furthermore, our framework offers several important advantages over other methods, including zero-resource learnability, lower data requirements, and better generalization to unseen data, all without requiring expert intervention. The source code for this project can be accessed through the following GitHub link: https://github.com/ghr1426/Neural-Task-Depictions.

A widely-used technique for enhancing low-resolution video, Video Super-Resolution (VSR), has seen significant progress in recent years. A notable model, BasicVSR, which was introduced in 2020, has been a prominent achievement in the field, yielding superior results compared to other models of that time. This paper updates BasicVSR to yield even better results, using an improved network design and a more sophisticated method for aligning video frames. The updated model is called BasicVSR++, and it outperforms other video super-resolution models by a considerable margin, achieving higher accuracy and making use of auxiliary information more effectively.

Many practical applications in reinforcement learning come from operations research, particularly in inventory control, scheduling, and transportation. Tasks like these often require solving complex optimization models to produce the desired outcome. In a multi-task reinforcement learning framework, leveraging pre-existing solutions to these problems can significantly improve training efficiency, assuming some tasks remain unchanged. However, if the system is designed with a single, unified solution for all tasks, an expert task can compromise the learning process, causing the agent to produce low-quality output. To mitigate this issue, we propose a modular system where separate components handle different tasks, and the agent can selectively swap between these modules to avoid contamination. Through both theoretical justifications and practical evaluations, especially on a scheduling use case, our modular design proves to be more robust than a unified system.

Working in the laboratory, scientists can only observe and record data for a specific period due to equipment restrictions, leading to a common challenge in conducting experiments. In the field of experimental thermodynamics, this constraint often interferes with the investigation of systems that require infinite or quasi-static conditions. In this research, a theoretical approach is undertaken to study quantum systems undergoing a restricted thermal process, in order to identify operating protocols yielding maximum efficiency within a given time frame. The study focuses on a two-level system and determines the optimal working cycle, in addition to providing an inequality that measures the performance gap of a given cycle when compared to the ideal cycle within a given time frame. The research shows that optimal performance is achieved when the system undergoes a exponential transition, in addition to providing an understanding of how certain heat engine parameters are linked. The study provides a theoretical framework for determining essential parameters through experimental measurement, ultimately leading to a better comprehension of finite-time heat engine performance.

Extreme weather conditions such as hurricanes and tornadoes have a significant impact on energy production and distribution. To better understand their effect, it is essential to analyze their spatial and temporal patterns. In this study, we apply a novel approach to assessing spatial and temporal relationships, utilizing real-world data related to hurricanes and energy systems in the United States. Our results reveal that there is a notable correlation between the intensity of these storms and the severity of impacts on energy systems, highlighting the importance of considering weather events' anisotropy and temporality when designing mitigation strategies. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, we conduct case studies on power plants, grids, and wind farms, suggesting potential applications and improvements.

In this study, we prove a complex eigenfunction theorem for the Dirac operator within the framework of Clifford analysis. Specifically, we have derived a rigorous theorem demonstrating the unique three-sphere constraint on eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. This theorem is seen to be a rigorous equivalent to the constrained three-sphere theorem in the context of harmonic functions. Furthermore, we establish a converse theorem on eigenfunction constraints, extending the findings of Perelman's three-circle theorem. This work is particularly relevant to eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator and its square, obtained through the Clifford algebra, where connections to monogenic functions and their square have been discussed.

We develop a new theory for measuring disorder in multi-scale patterns with alternating sequences, building on the Dyck system and its subgroups. This subgroups' enumeration by McIntosh and the Hausdorff dimension of their orbit closure under map $T:X\to X$ give us two distinct measures of chaos, both quantifying error rates in patterns that follow a certain template. This new theory applies to a wide range of patterns, including those seen in watermelon patterns, as well as those created by iterating polynomials over the complex plane, and we use it to measure the level of disorder in these patterns. In the case of the tent map, both measures of chaos are found to be the same, but this is not the case for the sawtooth map, where they are found to be different, and even opposite, indicating that one is not necessarily a good indicator of the other. This new understanding of chaos measures also reveals a fundamental difference in how they behave when applied to certain sets of patterns, and this difference is linked to whether or not these patterns can be reached approachably, and what happens to them as they are scaled at varying rates.

In a scalar sector with two scalars where one is heavily coupled, we simulate the Higgs-like scalar's production and decay in the Standard Model and a variety of extensions, assuming the other scalar is much heavier. Typically, this longer-lived particle would have already been detected, leaving the coupled scalar's properties to be determined through measurement of the lighter particle's production and decay rates. However, certain models allow the indicator scalar to decay directly into the heavier one, potentially making the indicator undetectable even if the heavier scalar is observed. Our study focuses on these unusual cases, exploring the detectability of the indicator scalar in various models where it may decay into a pair of top-quarks, a pair of $\tau$-leptons, or a Higgs boson. Once the indicator scalar is found, it could serve as a tool to investigate the heavier scalar's properties, potentially allowing for the determination of the heavier scalar's mass, coupling, and branching ratios, even in scenarios where it cannot be directly detected.

This paper presents a generative framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an autoregressive raw waveform model, to produce quasi-periodic signals like speech and music. To enhance efficiency, the framework integrates a Pitch-sensitive Dilated Convolution neural network into the autoregressive WaveNet architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that the QPWNet model can generate signals with a longer period than the AR-WN approach, specifically for speech and music with a period of up to 100ms. Moreover, the proposed framework achieves a higher overall quality than the AR-WN and StyleGAN-V2 models in terms of signal period, spectral smoothness, and naturalness.

The growing issue of information overload is complexly interconnected to the sparse nature of human preferences. To address this challenge, recommendation systems can be viewed as decoding the underlying preferences of users, which are embedded within the complete space of available items. From a user-centric perspective, our proposed BiclusterCF method utilizes biclusters - a combination of users and items - to enhance the discovery of cooperative patterns in preference data. By initially identifying row biclusters composed of highly similar users with varied interests towards a particular set of items, and subsequently extracting column biclusters characterized by high consistency across multiple users, BiclusterCF effectively uncovers the inherent structure of user preferences. As a result, users can discover novel, relevant items from the system, while reducing the impact of data scarcity and accurately reflecting the subjective nature of human preferences. Our framework's integration of BiclusterCF with existing CF methods further validates its effectiveness in improving performance and addressing the inherent sparse nature of human preferences.

The Rosetti index, a newly identified indium-based index, was found to be strongly affected by solar magnetic activity in a study that analyzed data from HARPS-N. By using a spectral influence approach, the study investigated the impact of solar activity on inductive indices, including the Rosetti index, and established a relationship between these indices and solar faculae and faculae-free areas on the sun's surface. However, the study found that the inductive indices were not directly indicative of solar magnetic activity. Faculae-rich regions were found to have stronger absorption lines, but the study could not establish a direct connection between these features and magnetic regions. Therefore, the study could not conclude that the inductive indices were influenced by solar magnetic activity in a meaningful way.

In probing Majorana modes through local tunneling spectroscopy, the signature peak often becomes obscured by a vast zero-bias conductance, making identification a challenge. A new technique has been proposed to rectify this issue by employing a resistive tunneling contact that modulates the tunneling density of states, resulting in the Majorana peak emerging more distinctly. This method has been demonstrated using a numerical model based on a hybrid spin-orbit qubit combined with a resistive tunnel contact. By adjusting the resistive contact's resistance, the typical zero-bias peak gives way to a broader, more defined resonance that can be asymmetric. This predicted resonance resembles the signature peak observed in experiments, such as those conducted on InAs/Al nanowires. This method offers a potential solution for confirming the presence of Majorana modes through experimental observation.

Marking a object in a category D by a projection from another object B gives rise to a bicategorical sum, a concept applied to various mathematical structures such as functors, modules, and so on. For half-bundles in differential geometry, such a marking is equivalent to a section with specific characteristics. The concept of shading (or "ombre") a category D by using B is a more general version of this marking, involving an equivariant map from B to D. Shading a category can be seen as a way to extend it. The showering of a category is similar, using equivariant maps with specific properties, and is related to shaded functors. By applying shading and showering to various mathematical structures, several key theorems can be proven and their consequences determined. For example, the concept of shading is used to demonstrate the existence of certain functors, such as a shaded functor from the category of manifolds to the category of shaded functors. Similarly, the concept of showering is used to demonstrate the existence of certain functors, such as a showered funktor from the category of shaded functors to the category of functors.

We've developed a novel approach to tone mapping that extracts a style from a collection of images, enabling both global tone mapping and reverse tone mapping. By identifying a signature style from a set of images, we can generate a transformation that maps arbitrary images into this style, achieving our goal of tone mapping. This style-extraction approach is flexible and can be adapted to various objective functions, but intriguingly, we've discovered that using a data-driven average with robust scaling yields superior results. Our method allows for the first time to accurately recover the original luminance values from a lone tone-mapped image, a previously unsolvable problem. We've further combined our style-extraction approach with a neural network that estimates luminance values, and the result is a seamless integration that enables high-quality tone mapping. We've formally proved the existence of our style-extraction approach and conducted extensive experiments to demonstrate its superior performance over existing methods, even when applied to a single image for the first time.

This technical report outlines the rules and evaluation protocol for the AQTC task, which is one of the three track B challenges at the LOVEU competition hosted at CVPR 2022. The protocol details how video clips were selected, labeled, and divided into training and testing sets, as well as the criteria and methods used for evaluating task performance.

Observations of atmospheric turbulence over the past decade have consistently shown that temperatures below the freezing point are divided into two distinct layers with vertical temperature gradients in the upper layer and parallel to the ground in the lower layer, a phenomenon observed worldwide, regardless of weather and season. This research provides the first experimental demonstration that temperatures below freezing are selectively "swept" as warm and cold air masses alternate at the boundary between these two layers in conjunction with snowfall. Utilizing high-speed cameras in snow-covered forests during both natural and artificial snowfall conditions, the study revealed detailed insights into the dynamics of temperature gradients and the relationship between particle collisions and temperature changes in the upper atmospheric layer. The research also shows that the same thermal behavior can be replicated by shooting water droplets at each other in a controlled environment, thus linking the atmospheric turbulence phenomena to collisions and providing a new understanding of the dynamics of temperature gradients in the upper atmospheric layer.

The intelligent robot navigation problem can be described as a type of hybrid planning system where a robot strives to accomplish tasks, such as reaching a specific goal, while adhering to specific rules to ensure a safe movement. Inspired by logic that operates in a forward-chaining manner, this paper proposes a new method called Active Deduction, which operates in a backward-feeding sequence. The goal of this method is to make use of the robot's sensory capabilities, which provide real-time data, by incorporating them into the sensing capability itself. The efficiency of this approach is confirmed through a simulation test, which demonstrates that it results in a significant reduction in the vast number of deductive steps traditionally associated with logic-based methods.

In applications like LiDAR 3D sensor data analysis, managing large volumes of data effectively becomes a significant challenge. Current data reduction techniques, mainly using statistical methods, fail to account for data's complex interrelations. Recent research has relied on machine learning, specifically deep neural networks, but these methods learn irrelevant features, effectively wasting computational resources. To address this issue, we introduce a data reduction framework that utilizes a autoencoder structure, incorporating two convolutional layers in the encoder and two convolutional layers with bilateral training in the decoder. This framework not only minimizes feature extraction errors but also directly optimizes reconstruction error. Through testing on LiDAR 3D data, we demonstrate our method outperforms conventional data reduction techniques and maintains comparable performance in classification tasks.

In the Finzi model of gravity, matter particles have an additional, quantum-like degree of freedom which interacts with the gravitational field. This model predicts that gravitational fields within galaxy clusters will take on discrete, step-like forms. Researchers conducted an in-depth analysis of the relationship between the quantum-like degree of freedom and the gravitational strength within simulated galaxy clusters. Their findings match previous observations of the distribution of galaxy clusters, including the likelihood of larger clusters containing more galaxies. The analysis was repeated for different levels of gravity strength and revealed that certain properties, such as the distribution of galaxy numbers within clusters of a given mass, do not depend on gravity strength. Conversely, other properties, such as the rates at which new galaxies form within clusters and the ranges of gravitational strengths found within clusters, do vary depending on gravity strength. The variations in these last two properties, however, can be predicted using a simplified theoretical model. The study demonstrates that, despite its differing physical underpinnings, the Finzi model can simultaneously agree with two different sets of observational data, the King model's predictions for gravitational strength and the numerous galaxy mass functions. The study's results, however, do not yet align with a further set of observational data related to the rates of galaxy formation and the distribution of dark matter within galaxy clusters.

A type of geometric hypergraph called convex geometric hypergraph CGH consists of a set of subsets originating from strictly convex sets in the Euclidean space. In a recent study, researchers compared the total number of subsets in a CGH with the total number of subsets in a geometric hypergraph GH, showcasing that the former can exceed the latter by an exponentially increasing difference as the size of the underlying sets grows larger. This significant discrepancy is attributed to the presence of a particular type of geometric hypergraph called QGH. Additionally, researchers established a criterion to distinguish CGHs from QGHs, and, using this criterion, they demonstrated that the previously established lower bound for the total number of subsets in a QGH is also the least possible. This new finding presents an improved distinction between CGHs and QGHs, offering more refined insights into their characteristics.

To understand how to apply the reductive method to calculate the cross-sections of nuclear reactions below the threshold of the weakly bound systems, the density of the inclusive cross-section of the $^{6}$Li + $^{51}$V system at an energy near the Coulomb barrier is calculated using a classical and quantum approach. This is done by applying the reductive method to a non-trivial case, which includes accounting for the significant deformation of both nuclei. The results show that this method can effectively determine the inclusive cross-section, and the differences between the calculated values from the classical and quantum approach mainly occur due to the Li target's non-spherical shape. Additionally, the liabilities of the reductive method over other methods such as three-body scattering are discussed.

Our research focuses on the Pacific lamprey's decision-making process for ascending towards their ultimate feeding and breeding destinations, which are located far inland at low salt levels. We made a breakthrough by discovering that the lamprey's navigational ability is not dependent on visual inputs, but rather uses a unique magnetic-field-sensitive organ. During an experiment, we submerged Pacific lamprees in a tank with two distinct sections: one with reduced magnetic field readings and another with optimized readings matching their natural environment. The results showed that the lamprees strongly prefer and strongly avoid certain magnetic field configurations, but only if they are within a specific range of salt levels. Based on these findings, we created a mathematical model that explains their ascending behavior. We also conducted a detailed analysis to determine the most effective salinity levels for capturing Pacific lamprees in the Columbia River Basin, which could potentially impact their population numbers and distribution patterns.

The ongoing struggle for colon cancer treatment is driven by the growing number of patients and the limited effectiveness of existing methods. As an alternative to standard treatments, immunotherapy holds promise for potential cures, which could be further optimized through individualized medical approaches. By modeling this process using a Fokker-Planck framework, researchers created a simulation tool to guide current cancer therapy and identify more effective treatment methods. The primary goal of this study was to develop an individualized treatment plan that would maximize the survival rate of colon cancer patients by simulating the immune system's response to different therapies. The results of these simulations revealed the potential for improved patient outcomes by combining existing treatments in a customized manner, which could also enable the identification of novel cancer-specific targets. The research employed a stochastic process to simulate the interaction between the immune system and colon cancer cells, utilizing a nonlinear Schrödinger equation and its corresponding Fokker-Planck version. The individualized treatment plans were based on an optimization technique that maximizes patient survival, which could also be applied to other types of cancer. The research has the potential to be widely applied to clinical settings, where it could be used to improve treatment outcomes.

The surge in mobile device usage has led to a steady growth in wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication adoption. As demand for seamless video streaming, augmented reality, and virtual reality services drives networks to capacity, conventional wireless communication methods may no longer be sufficient. To address these challenges, researchers are developing new strategies, such as network function optimization, that could revolutionize D2D communication. A promising approach is being developed by China Mobile Communications Corporation, where real-time device scheduling through deep learning methods could enable the creation of self-organizing networks. This novel scheduling method would empower operators to efficiently manage resources, tackle complex interference issues, and achieve optimal performance. To illustrate the effectiveness of this idea, the authors present simulated results showing significant gains in overall network performance and efficiency.

We demonstrate that the helicity, specifically defined as the volume integral of the dot product of the velocity and curl of the velocity in three-dimensional space, remains constant over time for solutions obtained from solving the compressible Euler equations. This finding applies to fluids with any internal structure as long as they are non-viscous and in a state of equilibrium. Furthermore, the helicity can be shown to be conserved analytically using the Lagrangian method, which involves applying the Euler-Lagrange equations to a specially crafted action integral.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we have developed a framework for approximating the reflection coefficient near singular points on the bulk edges of the associated Jacobi matrices.  In particular, we have derived asymptotic formulas for the reflection coefficient as $k$ approaches large values, and our results reveal a $|k|^3$ dependence on the magnitude of $k$.  Our work is guided by a method that was initially used to study singular continuous spectrum in quasiperiodic systems; this approach involves analyzing nearly periodic 1D tight-binding models.

Analyzing the impact of gravitational waves on binary compact systems, such as neutron star binaries, reveals the influence of pre-existing orbital misalignments. These alignments can be attributed to various factors, including residual eccentricities remaining from the ancestors of these binaries. To investigate the extent of remaining eccentricities, we considered the effects of gravitational waves, tidal forces, and velocity dispersion within the galactic environment, applying accurate estimates through post-Newtonian analysis. Our research indicates that initial alignments ranging from 10^-5 to 10^-3 can be accounted for, with eccentricities decreasing as stellar environments become denser. These findings are summarized in tabular form for different stellar environments.

A breakthrough technique to produce intense coherent X-ray flashes has been developed by combining a free-electron laser oscillator with a special undulator, which amplifies the oscillation to increase its energy, resulting in high luminosity and output powers. The procedure is explained through detailed simulations which also measured the current limitations imposed by technical factors such as beam contamination and energy loss. The experimental setup, using the existing DESY facility, achieved the production of 6.5 Hz X-ray flashes at a wavelength of 7.5 nm, reaching a record high peak power and average power of 125 W and 18 mW respectively. The generated X-rays have a nearly perfect Gaussian profile with high polarization, making them ideal for a range of applications including advanced materials research, medical research and industrial applications.

When a virus spreads through a network of interconnected systems, detecting the source of the outbreak becomes a crucial task for containment. A research framework for identifying incidents that cause widespread malware propagation has been established and is now being further developed. Initially, the approach recognizes incident patterns by analyzing the malware's propagation rate over time within a virtual environment. Next, it generates predicted propagation curves for actual incidents and selects those that closely match the observed propagation speed. Finally, a simulation of different incident scenarios is run to determine which ones correspond to the actual incident, using the predicted propagation rates as a benchmark. This research will explore methods for refining incident identification by leveraging analysis of the system's performance metrics, such as process creation rates, to enhance accuracy.

The shock wave's collapse, a scenario where a shock fails to expand into a rarefied gas, has been a topic of interest among astrophysicists for decades, with applications to various phenomena such as star explosions and wind interactions. A comprehensive review of the issue is presented, focusing on the behavior of collapsing shocks at the boundary between two mediums of different densities. The article discusses key factors like pressure balance, the classification of collapsing shocks, and numerical simulations that inform our understanding of this complex process.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for signs of cancer, high-grade lesions, or areas of invasion. Traditionally, this process relied on manual, time-consuming histopathological analysis, but recent advancements in deep learning have made it feasible to automate this task. To facilitate further research in this area, a large dataset of UniToPatho images, along with manually annotated labels and regions of interest, has been made available. This resource can be leveraged to develop and train effective deep learning strategies for both classification and grading tasks.

In the context of information theory, we're exploring a newcomer to the field, called data leakage, which refers to the amount of information that can be extracted from a source with a protected secret, beyond its inherent entropy. Our analysis is centered around two fundamental constraints: one related to leakage tolerance and another related to zero-error encoding. Utilizing graph theory, we've developed new approaches to tackle these problems, which also offer valuable insights to researchers working on leakage-free coding systems. This framework allows us to gain insight into the general relationships between leakage tolerance and zero-error encoding constraints. Furthermore, we're able to identify the specific features of graph structures that enable optimal leakage control, which also offers potential applications in coding design.

Enhancing the resolution of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images is critical due to the inherent trade-off between image resolution and the distance of the radar sensor from the target. Existing methods, such as classical image processing techniques and machine learning algorithms, often fall short in effectively improving resolution while preserving details. To address this, a novel deep learning-based approach called MrSARP is proposed, which leverages a bi-directional hierarchical architecture consisting of a top-down feature extraction module and a bottom-up generator. This approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in enhancing non-existent radar configurations based on existing information. The key innovations of MrSARP include its novel multi-resolution feature extraction module and the efficient learning of patch translation, which significantly improves performance. The development and performance of MrSARP were validated using the fully polarized ERC-1030 radar, which is widely used in various applications. The detailed design and configuration of MrSARP, as well as its trained model, will be made publicly available to facilitate future research and implementation.

A variational approach known as Variational Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (VQAAO) has been proposed as a more efficient alternative to Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). However, noisy data from noisy quantum computations hinders the performance of VQAAO and QAOA. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an improved method, Bayesian Enhancement for QAOA (BEQ), which effectively handles noisy data from noisy quantum computations. BEQ utilizes Bayesian estimation to calculate parameter expectations in noisy quantum circuits, thereby enhancing its performance. In experiments, BEQ has demonstrated significant improvements over VQAA and QAOA, achieving notable results with up to 430% improvement in success rates in certain situations using noisy quantum circuits.

This research explores the computational challenges of processing intersection points between two ellipses, a topic relevant to designing photonic integrated circuits and semiconductor laser diodes. The study identifies three areas where the intersection points cluster: one region contains zero points and the other two contain either one or two points each. The conditions required for the intersection points to gather in each of these areas are established and the associated calculation complexities are analyzed. The findings can be utilized to develop more efficient algorithms for the approximate calculation of ellipse intersections, with the goal of optimizing processing in integrated circuits to minimize computational load.

The concept of q-training is normally applied in a stationary environment, but we now consider its application in a dynamic setting. In a situation where the surroundings are constantly changing, it's challenging to maintain a stable reinforcement learning strategy. To overcome this issue, we can model the ever-changing surroundings using a so-called "drifting state space" and develop a q-training method that automatically adjusts to these shifting conditions. Our proposed solution can function autonomously, requiring no input from a human operator to update its policy, thus enhancing the system's self-improvement capabilities. Additionally, we can use the drifting state space model to simulate a stable environment, which provides a theoretical foundation for our approach.

A numerical investigation based on the self-consistent functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been conducted to extend the analysis of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice, accounting for higher-order inter-neighbor interactions. The triangular lattice is a prototypical model for studying magnetic ground states. In this study, the impact of additional interaction terms on the Fermi surface and the phase diagram has been examined, focusing specifically on the competition it induces between different types of long-range magnetic orders. The presence of non-local magnetic oscillations, a hallmark of the Fermi liquid regime, has been used to determine the relative importance of different momentum components. The results show that the magnetic oscillations' amplitude, relative to the leading component, varies significantly with the presence of additional interactions. The investigation reveals a novel phase diagram, where the preferred type of long-range magnetic order shifts based on the level of interaction, from an antiferromagnetic state at moderate interactions to a nematic state with broken rotational symmetry at stronger interactions. The study finds that this transition is an example of the 'order-by-disorder' phenomenon, where disorder (in this case, caused by interactions) induces a change in order.

Accurate vertebrae localization is a critical initial step in spinal surgery planning and related computer research. However, automatically localizing all vertebrae can be very challenging due to the low contrast of adjacent vertebrae in lumbar CT images. To address this problem, we propose a new method that utilizes a spinal reconstruction technique to enhance and automate vertebrae localization. Specifically, we divide the lumbar region into segments and use a neural network to pose each segment with a spinal axis, effectively transforming it to align with the upper adjacent segment's spinal canal. This alignment is based on anatomically-related landmarks such as the sacrum, sacroiliac joints, and L5 vertebral body. Once the lumbar segments are aligned, adjacent vertebrae are distinguishable due to their distinct positions, and a machine learning model is then trained to select the vertebrae centers. We evaluated our method on a dataset of 502 lumbar CT images and observed that it achieves high accuracy rates, with scores of 0.937 for center detection, 0.884 for regression-based vertebral body detection, and 0.775 for full vertebral body recognition.

This investigation explores the variability of currents within a theoretical framework of random thermodynamics and assesses the variability of currents within this model. By establishing a general formula for the variability of currents, we examine the asymptotic behavior of this expression in both linear and nonlinear systems. We demonstrate that the variability of currents in the random thermodynamics model adheres to a universal law, yielding a gauge-invariant distribution, which can be represented as the product of two factors. One factor corresponds to the variability of currents in non-interacting systems, whereas the other factor depends on the specific interactions within the system. We further clarify the relationship between the results obtained from this theoretical framework and existing findings from literature, which focus on the distinct cases of nonlinear interactions in the absence of external driving forces and periodic driving forces.

This research examines the relative quantum homology of a compact, real Kaehler manifold paired with a finite group, employing the established parameter $I$ to distinguish between homology and quantum versions. Our key finding reveals that the relative quantum homology remains unaffected by rational transformations, which aligns with a parallel observation made by Cohen and Koehler in the context of the traditional quantum homology. Furthermore, this study also explores the relationship between the relative quantum homology and the relative Euler characteristic.

The interaction of acoustic waves between nearby, directly coupled crystals is
of great interest for both scientific study and practical application. Our
theoretical framework provides a basis for acoustic wave transmission
characterization between two piezoelectric materials, incorporating effects of
insulating layers, wave frequency, and crystal orientation. By experimenting
with various material combinations and configurations, we demonstrate that a
specific setup featuring a 2-micrometer gap and highly polarizable materials
results in exceptionally high transmission levels, frequently exceeding 90%.
The observed transmission properties can be attributed to the alignment of the
piezoelectric materials and the near-field acoustic coupling behavior. Moreover,
we have encountered a number of applications where this unique acoustic property
can be utilized.

We introduce a cutting-edge method based on the resonance of a microcavity-driven system that manipulates and regulates light propagation through a highly controlled and controlled process. A spontaneous phase-transition occurs within the system, resulting in the coexistence of two distinct types of quasiparticles: photon and exciton-polariton. The interaction between these quasiparticles enables the transfer of photon information into an optical signal that can be controlled and guided. The resulting photonic signal exhibits distinct characteristics of wave propagation, such as non-local interactions and tunable coherent behaviors. The system's ability to process optical information efficiently makes it suitable for use in optical neurocomputing and other photonic systems that support quantum computing.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays behavior that shifts dramatically between two distinct observing campaigns by Spitzer, which saw the emergence of a new pattern of periodic drops in transit and unusual color changes. As the transit depth diminishes, the longer wavelengths show deeper drops and a shift towards red coloration. Observations by the Large Binocular Telescope's NIRC2 and PHAENEX camera reveal tentative evidence for a diminutive secondary eclipse preceding the primary transit at two separate occasions. The observed shifts can be explained by the ongoing disintegration of the exoplanet as larger grains navigate through the atmosphere, altering the transit depth and ground-based observations confirming the presence of grains in space, which were initially detected by Spitzer. The increased mass loss and larger grain sizes contradict theoretical smooth particle mesh models generated by Simulate Prime, which had predicted a specific mass loss rate based on the initial grain sizes. As a result, there's growing evidence that smaller grains are navigated through the atmosphere en route to the ground, whereas larger grains require a closer examination of the atmosphere dynamics to understand their behavior and fate.

We demonstrate a novel coherence for the Milnor fiber of a singular point on a variety, tied to the flatness of a particular key boundary. This key boundary consists of singular points with specific types of singularities on a larger variety, and its name reflects its importance in analyzing the Milnor fiber. The proposed coherence has significant implications in several areas: the parameters in the Milnor model are finite in number; the determinant of the monodromy matrix can be expressed as an eigenvalue of a larger matrix; and the ability to consider the asymptotic scaling of interactions in a particular context. Additionally, this coherence implies the existence of distinct components within the Milnor fiber, and the parameters that define them can be identified by analyzing a related system.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform library for cross-platform data analysis. It's currently available under the MIT license and offers a wide range of statistical methods in the vein of R, but with a strong focus on.NET compatibility. This allows Daany to seamlessly integrate with.NET languages such as C#, F#, VB.NET, and IronPython. At its core, Daany utilizes the tabular data model to provide efficient data manipulation and analysis capabilities. A tabular data model represents data as a collection of rows and columns, with inherent benefits for data analysis. This tabular data model effectively eliminates the need for explicit data typing, significantly speeding up computation. Daany also supports various data storage solutions, including in-memory storage, SQL, CSV, and JSON. This enables developers to choose their preferred storage solution for their projects. As a result, Daany offers a wide range of applications, including but not limited to, data analysis, machine learning, data-driven UI development, and data-driven serverless workflows. This project aims to bring Daany to a broader audience, providing comprehensive documentation and guidelines for optimal usage.

The controversy surrounding the comet of 1577 brought mathematicians and philosophers into dispute. Philosophers argued that celestial bodies must remain eternally moving, as they are divine and unchanging. Mathematicians, however, disputed this, citing the comet's clear visibility with the naked eye. This paper explores the conflict between mathematical and philosophical views on the nature of the universe, with the comet of 1577 serving as a focal point. The unexpected alliance of mathematicians against philosophers reveals a shift in the shifting balance of mathematical and philosophical powers during the Renaissance.

The primary goal of this research was to examine how non-Gaussian characteristics affect ionization processes in the early universe. Building on past work by Saha, we established equations to examine a particular interaction between particles, derived from a model based on non-Gaussian distributions of electrons and a constant radiation pressure. Our findings indicate that when the electron distribution is not perfectly symmetric, the relationship between the mean photon frequency and the square root of the electron density no longer applies. Additionally, we discovered that as long as certain physical conditions are met, the mean photon frequency will decrease during the ionization process. Our study also demonstrates how a particular ratio of photon and electron energies influences the mean photon frequency, potentially leading to inaccurate estimates of the mean photon frequency if this ratio is not taken into account.

The managed integration of two magnetohydrodynamic codes, one simulating a tokamak core and the other the edge, has allowed for an in-depth examination of magnetic island formation and merging in a two-island, quasi-stable internal mode configuration. Our study reveals that the interaction of these islands leads to the creation of a dynamic, electrostatic field that causes one island to collapse as another completes an orbit around it. As a result of electron acceleration within the merging region, a significant amount of heat is generated there. Our analysis of the kinetic effects on magnetohydrodynamics demonstrates that factoring in the behavior of individual particles using an integrated PIC-MHD model offers a more comprehensive understanding of the process than an MHD simulation alone can provide.

This paper presents Amanuensis, an innovative autonomous learning system designed to educate human teachers how to write code for a specific machine learning model. Amanuensis takes a unique approach, utilizing its autonomous judgments to correct human mistakes during code development, rather than relying on human-in-the-loop methods. By making these autonomous corrections, Amanuensis demonstrates that its internal logic is the correct course of action. Our experimental findings apply to a particular teaching model but are broadly generalizable to other similar scenarios.
